The Thursday club met in the gym of the Halverson Rec Center, six green tables in two rows, and Nadia had been coming for four months. She played the way she had taught herself in her cousin's garage: stand close, wait for anything high, and hit it hard. Most of the players her age had learned to stay out of her way.

The sign-up sheet that week put her against a man named Mr. Esposito, who looked about seventy and wore a cardigan over his club shirt. He stood a long way back from the table, almost against the gym wall, and warmed up by chopping the ball low over the net with a slicing, downward stroke. Nadia had seen men play like that in the park, patting the ball back and forth with their coffee cups on the bench, and she decided the match would be short.

She won the first two points with smashes. Then every ball began to come back. She would hit as hard as she could, and Mr. Esposito would drift sideways, chop, and send the ball floating back, slow and low and spinning backward. When she hit it flat, it dropped into the net. When she hit it harder, it dropped into the net faster. She lost the first game eleven to four.

Between games she sat on the bottom bleacher with the scorecard her friend Tomás had been keeping. He marked every point with a letter, the way their coach had shown them: W for a winner, N for a ball in the net, L for one that went long. Down her side of the card ran a column that was nearly all N's.

"He isn't beating you," Tomás said. "The net is."

Nadia thought about the spin. A ball spinning backward would dive down off her paddle unless she lifted it. So in the second game she stopped trying to end every rally with one stroke. She brushed under the ball and pushed it back, deep and low, and pushed again, and waited. Sometimes eight or nine strokes went by before Mr. Esposito sent one back a little too high. Then she hit it.

She won the second game eleven to nine. The third game went to deuce, and she lost it on a push that clipped the top of the net and fell back on her own side.

Mr. Esposito came around the table to shake her hand. He told her that most people took a whole season to stop hitting into his net, and some never did. Then he asked whether she would be there next Thursday.

On the bus home Nadia turned the scorecard over. On the back, in pencil, she began a list of the things she had watched him do that she could not yet do: stand far back without losing ground, chop with a loose wrist, and wait for the right ball as though he had all afternoon.

At twelve the bells at Saint Anne's begin,
and the doors of the towers on Market Street
open like drawers pulled out all at once,
and the people come down into the light.

They carry paper bags and folded napkins,
a pear, a sandwich cut in half,
and climb the wide steps of the library
to sit where they sat yesterday.

The woman with the crossword takes the fourth step,
left of the stone lion, always the left.
Two men in work boots share
a bag of oranges and say almost nothing.
The boy from the bike shop eats standing up.

I take the top step by the column
with my soup in its paper cup,
and for an hour the stone is warm
and the street smells of bread and diesel.

Nobody here has asked my name,
and I have kept from asking theirs,
but I know the crossword woman works in ink
and the men in boots peel oranges in one long curl.

One Tuesday the fourth step stood empty.
I ate my soup and watched the doors.
The pigeons worked the place where she would be,
and the clock on the bank moved slowly.

On Wednesday she was back, a bandage on one wrist,
the paper folded to the puzzle,
and I was surprised how glad I was to see her,
someone I could not have named.

At one the bells again. The bags are folded,
the crumbs brushed off for the birds,
and the steps empty from the bottom up,
the way a glass empties, the way a room does

when everyone has somewhere to be.
Tomorrow at twelve the drawers will open.
We will climb to the places we have kept for each other
without a word about keeping them.

My mother made scallion pancakes every Saturday morning, and for most of my childhood I assumed the recipe was written down somewhere. The summer I turned eleven, I asked for it so that I could make them on my own, and she looked at me as though I had asked for the instructions for walking.

"Flour," she said. "Hot water. Scallions. Salt. Oil."

"How much flour?"

She held out her two hands, cupped together. "This much."

So the next Saturday I stood beside her at the counter with a big measuring jug, a set of spoons, and the green notebook I used for science. Each time she reached for something, I asked her to stop. I tipped her double handful of flour into the jug and wrote down two and a half cups. I had filled the kettle myself, so when she had finished adding hot water, I measured what was left, took it away from what I had started with, and wrote down one cup. She let me do it, though it doubled the time the pancakes took, and twice she laughed so hard at the sight of me chasing her hand with a teaspoon that she had to put down the rolling pin.

By the end of the morning I had a page of numbers. Two weeks later, while my mother was at work, I followed them exactly. The dough came out wet and stuck to everything: the bowl, the counter, my fingers. I kept adding flour until it stopped sticking, and the pancakes came out as tough as cardboard. I ate one, threw the rest away, and said nothing.

She found out anyway, from the flour I had missed on the floor under the stove. She asked what had gone wrong, and I showed her the page. She read it through, and then she asked what kind of day it had been. I thought she meant my mood.

It had rained for three days, she said, and on damp days the flour was already holding water from the air, so the dough needed less. Her hands had never been measuring the flour. They had been measuring the dough. She poured the water in a little at a time, and kneaded, and stopped when the dough came away clean from the bowl, and what that took in cups was different every Saturday.

I still have the green notebook. The page of numbers is crossed out with a single line, and under it, in my own handwriting from that summer, is the recipe I use now. There are almost no numbers in it. It says: hot water, a little at a time. Knead until it stops sticking to the bowl. If it has been raining, start with less.

"Flour," she said. "Hot water. Scallions. Salt. Oil."

"How much flour?"

She held out her two hands, cupped together. "This much."

I tipped her double handful of flour into the jug and wrote down two and a half cups. I had filled the kettle myself, so when she had finished adding hot water, I measured what was left, took it away from what I had started with, and wrote down one cup. She let me do it, though it doubled the time the pancakes took, and twice she laughed so hard at the sight of me chasing her hand with a teaspoon that she had to put down the rolling pin.

By the end of the morning I had a page of numbers. Two weeks later, while my mother was at work, I followed them exactly. The dough came out wet and stuck to everything: the bowl, the counter, my fingers. I kept adding flour until it stopped sticking, and the pancakes came out as tough as cardboard. She found out anyway, from the flour I had missed on the floor under the stove. She asked what had gone wrong, and I showed her the page. She read it through, and then she asked what kind of day it had been. I thought she meant my mood.

It had rained for three days, she said, and on damp days the flour was already holding water from the air, so the dough needed less. Her hands had never been measuring the flour. They had been measuring the dough. She poured the water in a little at a time, and kneaded, and stopped when the dough came away clean from the bowl, and what that took in cups was different every Saturday.

I still have the green notebook. The page of numbers is crossed out with a single line, and under it, in my own handwriting from that summer, is the recipe I use now. When I was growing up, my family could argue about a single fact for a week. Is Rome farther north than New York? My uncle said obviously not, since Rome was warm and New York had blizzards. My mother said she had read somewhere that it was the other way around. My sister, who was nine, said the two cities were probably at about the same place and everyone should stop shouting.

Nobody in the house could settle it. So for days the question came back at dinner, and each time someone had a new piece of evidence. My uncle remembered that oranges grew in Italy. My mother pointed out that the ocean keeps some coasts warmer than their position on the globe would suggest. On Sunday my uncle brought over a road atlas so old that several countries in it had since changed their names, and we spread it across the table and ran our fingers along the lines of latitude. Rome was farther north, by a little more than a degree. My uncle insisted the atlas was out of date.

Today that argument would last about eight seconds. Someone would ask the question, someone else would type it into a phone, and the answer would arrive, correct and complete, before my uncle had finished his first sentence about blizzards.

I do not want to pretend this is a loss in every way. A wrong belief corrected in eight seconds is better than a wrong belief held for life, and my uncle went on insisting for years. But something did disappear when we started settling every question on the spot, and it took me a while to see what it was.

What disappeared was the middle part, the part between the question and the answer. That week of dinners was a week of reasoning. We weighed climate against geography, decided which memories to trust, and tried to picture a map from memory. My sister's guess, that the two cities were close, turned out to be nearer the truth than either adult's. None of that happens when the answer arrives first. A phone tells you what is true. It is silent on how you might have worked it out, or how near you came on your own.

So my family now has a rule, borrowed in spirit from that old atlas. When a question comes up at dinner, everyone gets ten minutes to argue before anyone may reach for a phone. Most nights the phone wins in the end, as it should. But by then we have usually found out something the phone could never have told us: what each of us thought, and why.

In the fall of 1914, the only public transportation in Granger Falls was the streetcar line that ran down Main Street from the depot to the woolen mills, a route of about three miles. The cars came every twenty minutes, and the fare was five cents. People who lived on the hill streets east of Main walked down to catch them, and in the rain they walked back up.

That November a mechanic named Orrin Platt began driving his secondhand touring car up and down Main Street a few minutes ahead of the streetcar. He would stop for anyone who waved, carry them anywhere along the line, and charge them a nickel, a coin that in the slang of the time was called a jitney. Within weeks the name had passed from the coin to the car. For the same fare, his passengers could be let off at their own doors on the hill streets, which the streetcar never climbed.

By spring, the town clerk counted more than forty jitneys on Main Street. Most were driven by men who owned a car and had a few hours to spare in the morning and evening, the busiest times of day. They kept no schedule. They ran when the crowds did and went home when the crowds thinned, leaving the streetcar to carry the riders of midday and late evening, when it earned the least.

The Granger Falls Traction Company, which owned the streetcars, saw its fares fall by nearly a third in six months. Its president, Howard Beal, went before the town council with a list of complaints. The jitneys, he said, chose the profitable hours and left the rest to his company; they carried no insurance, leaving an injured passenger to pay his own doctor; and they crowded the street so thickly that his motormen could barely keep to their timetable.

The council's answer, passed in the summer of 1915, required every jitney driver to buy a license, post a bond of five hundred dollars against accidents, and run a fixed route for at least twelve hours a day. Few drivers could meet those terms. Within a year, fewer than five jitneys were left, and the streetcar's fares had nearly recovered.

Yet the jitneys left something behind. Riders had learned that a vehicle could come to them rather than the other way around, and they had learned it on the hill streets that the rails had always passed by. When the Traction Company replaced its streetcars with motor buses in 1929, the first new route it drew ran up the hill east of Main, along the streets where Orrin Platt had once let people off at their doors.

That November a mechanic named Orrin Platt began driving his secondhand touring car up and down Main Street a few minutes ahead of the streetcar. He would stop for anyone who waved, carry them anywhere along the line, and charge them a nickel, a coin that in the slang of the time was called a jitney. Within weeks the name had passed from the coin to the car. For the same fare, his passengers could be let off at their own doors on the hill streets, which the streetcar never climbed.

By spring, the town clerk counted more than forty jitneys on Main Street. Most were driven by men who owned a car and had a few hours to spare in the morning and evening, the busiest times of day. They kept no schedule. They ran when the crowds did and went home when the crowds thinned, leaving the streetcar to carry the riders of midday and late evening, when it earned the least.

The council's answer, passed in the summer of 1915, required every jitney driver to buy a license, post a bond of five hundred dollars against accidents, and run a fixed route for at least twelve hours a day. In the 1670s, astronomers at the Paris Observatory were busy timing the moons of Jupiter. The innermost of the four large moons, Io, circles the planet about once every forty-two and a half hours, and on each trip around it passes into Jupiter's shadow and vanishes from view. Because these disappearances, called eclipses, come so regularly, astronomers hoped to use them as a clock in the sky, one that mapmakers in distant places could read to work out where on Earth they stood.

A Danish astronomer named Ole Rømer noticed that the clock seemed to run unevenly. During the months when Earth, moving along its own orbit, was drawing closer to Jupiter, the eclipses of Io came a little earlier than the tables predicted. During the months when Earth was moving away, they came later. The difference grew slowly, eclipse after eclipse, until it amounted to several minutes.

There was no obvious reason why a moon of Jupiter should keep different time depending on where Earth happened to be. Rømer's explanation was that the moon was keeping perfect time and the delay was in the message. Light, he proposed, takes time to travel. When Earth is farther from Jupiter, the light carrying news of an eclipse has farther to go, and so it reaches the telescope later.

In 1676 he made a public prediction: an eclipse of Io due that November would be seen about ten minutes later than the official tables said. It was. From timings like his, astronomers of the day estimated that light needs roughly twenty-two minutes to cross the full width of Earth's orbit.

That figure was too large. The modern value is closer to seventeen minutes, which works out to a speed of about 300,000 kilometers per second. But the error matters less than the idea. Before Rømer, many scholars assumed that light arrived everywhere at once. After him, light was a traveler with a speed that could be measured, even if the first measurement was rough.

It is worth noticing what Rømer lacked. Sending a beam of light to Jupiter and timing its return was far beyond anyone's reach in his century. What he had instead was a regular event far away, years of careful observations, and the willingness to take a small, stubborn mismatch seriously instead of blaming it on his instruments.

During the months when Earth was moving away, they came later. The difference grew slowly, eclipse after eclipse, until it amounted to several minutes.

There was no obvious reason why a moon of Jupiter should keep different time depending on where Earth happened to be. Rømer's explanation was that the moon was keeping perfect time and the delay was in the message. Light, he proposed, takes time to travel. When Earth is farther from Jupiter, the light carrying news of an eclipse has farther to go, and so it reaches the telescope later.

It is worth noticing what Rømer lacked. Sending a beam of light to Jupiter and timing its return was far beyond anyone's reach in his century.
